DeepH predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements for graphene with an average mean absolute error of 2.1 meV and a coefficient of determination r² = 0.9994 across all orbital combinations.
When applied to unseen graphene configurations sampled between 100 K and 400 K, DeepH maintains a mean absolute error of 1.9 meV for Hamiltonian matrix elements.

Band structures and electric susceptibility computed from DeepH for MoS₂ match DFT results closely.
DeepH generalizes to carbon nanotubes, achieving Hamiltonian prediction MAE below 3.5 meV for diameters larger than 2 nm and accurately reproducing their band structures.
DeepH scales linearly with system size and provides a three‑order‑of‑magnitude speed‑up over conventional DFT for a MoS₂ 35 × 35 supercell.

A DeepH model trained only on non‑twisted bilayer graphene structures predicts Hamiltonians for twisted bilayer graphene supercells up to ~1000 atoms with sub‑meV mean absolute error and correctly reproduces the flat‑band feature near the Fermi level at the magic angle (~1.08°).
DeepH accurately predicts DFT Hamiltonians and electronic properties for twisted bilayer bismuthene with strong spin‑orbit coupling, achieving errors comparable to those for twisted graphene.
Compared with empirical tight‑binding and continuum models, DeepH offers higher accuracy and transferability for twisted van‑der‑Waals materials, albeit with slightly lower computational efficiency.

DeepH can be applied to both periodic and non‑periodic systems, including three‑dimensional bulk carbon allotropes and quasi‑zero‑dimensional molecules, achieving sub‑meV mean absolute error for Hamiltonian predictions.
The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals.
The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%.
The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa).
Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene.

The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples.

Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations.

The Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA) GNN model achieves the lowest mean and variance of test mean‑squared error among GCN, GAT, and MPNN (sum and max) variants on the polycrystalline graphene dataset.
DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.

DeepH-E3 predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with sub‑meV mean absolute error, reducing the error by roughly a factor of two compared with the original DeepH method across diverse material systems.

DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.

DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.

DeepH‑E3 predicts a spin‑orbit‑coupling‑induced topological quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi₂Te₃, evidenced by band‑gap closing and reopening and a change of the Z₂ invariant from 0 to 1 as SOC strength increases.
DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.
DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.
The model generalizes to arbitrarily twisted bilayer structures; the mean absolute error of Hamiltonian predictions decreases as the Moiré supercell size grows (or twist angle decreases).
The model can fit 2.8 × 10⁹ non‑zero complex‑valued Hamiltonian matrix elements with only ~10⁵ real trainable parameters, indicating high capacity efficiency.

The workflow software FireWorks together with the custodian job‑management tool automatically manages high‑throughput DFT calculations, self‑heals failed runs, and applies material‑type‑specific workflows.
JARVIS-DFT contains approximately 40,000 materials and about 1 million calculated properties.
Beyond‑DFT methods (HSE06, PBE0, G0W0, DMFT) are generated for a subset of materials to provide higher‑level reference data and enable uncertainty quantification.
JARVIS‑Tools implements automatic k‑point convergence protocols that improve the precision of DFT calculations.
A REST‑API is provided for programmatic download and upload of JARVIS data, supporting community contributions and interoperability.
Inference with the MPNN takes roughly 10⁻² seconds per molecule, about 300,000 times faster than the DFT reference calculation (~10³ seconds).
The multiple‑tower architecture reduces the computational complexity of a propagation step from O(n²d²) to O(n²d²/k) and yields a 2× speedup for n=9, d=200, k=8.

The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.
AFLOW calculations follow a standardized sequential workflow: RELAX1 → RELAX2 → STATIC → BANDS for materials in the Elements, ICSD, and Heusler databases.
The PBE functional combined with PAW potentials is the default exchange-correlation functional and potential combination for ICSD, Binary Alloy, and Heusler databases.
DFT+U corrections are applied to the entire ICSD database and certain Heusler database entries containing O, S, Se, and F elements, but not to the Binary Alloy database.

Specific Ueff parameters are defined for d-block elements (Table 4) and U, J parameters for f-block elements (Table 5) to correct self-interaction error in DFT+U calculations, with values ranging from 1.9 eV (In) to 7.5 eV (Zn).
The AFLOWLIB data is accessible through a REST-API for standardized data exchange.

Matbench contains data from 10 density functional theory-derived and experimental sources including Materials Project, Zhuo et al., Landolt-Bornstein Handbook, Castelli et al., JARVIS DFT 2D, and Citrine Informatics.
DeepH resolves the accuracy‑efficiency dilemma of DFT, enabling efficient ab‑initio electronic‑structure calculations for large‑scale material systems.
AFLOW can automatically calculate a wide suite of physical observables across a large database of structures with minimal human intervention.

AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management.
Hybrid functional calculations scale approximately as O(N^2.5) for small systems and linearly beyond ~15 Å (HSE06) or ~100 Å (PBE0), whereas standard GGA calculations scale as O(N^3).
AFLOW implements DFT+U using the Dudarev formalism with default Ueff values for a wide range of elements.

L0-bal000005.surface_form: Benchmarking Materials Property Prediction Methods: The Matbench Test Set and Automatminer Reference Algorithm

Matbench v0.1 is a benchmark suite containing 13 supervised machine learning tasks (10 regression, 3 classification) for materials property prediction, with dataset sizes ranging from 312 to 132,752 samples.
Matbench tasks include predicting optical, thermal, electronic, thermodynamic, tensile, and elastic properties given materials composition and/or crystal structure.

Automatminer is a fully-automated machine learning pipeline consisting of four stages (autofeaturization, cleaning, dimensionality reduction, and AutoML search) that requires no user intervention or hyperparameter tuning.
Automatminer Express preset achieves the best performance on 8 of 13 tasks in the Matbench benchmark.
Automatminer's auto-generated models outperform or equal the Random Forest model across all Matbench tasks except predicting formation energies across the Materials Project.

Descriptor-based Automatminer and RF models have lower errors on small datasets but their improvement rates are shallower, with AutoML's advantage over conventional techniques narrowing as sample count increases and essentially lost near 10^5 samples.
All algorithms exhibit a universal trend of decreasing relative errors as dataset size increases.

For small datasets (<10^4 samples), inexpensive Automatminer presets (~1-5 minute training) retain the bulk of performance compared to expensive presets (24h+ training), with Express retaining 95% or more of the accuracy of more expensive presets at less than 50% of the computational cost on data-scarce tasks.

Matbench provides a consistent evaluation framework using five-fold nested cross-validation on identical folds across all algorithms to minimize comparison bias, with datasets pre-cleaned to remove unphysical computed data and task-irrelevant experimental data.
Automatminer source code and pre-processed Matbench tasks are open source and available online.

Training set cleaning procedures including minimum ion-ion distance cutoff, energy/force outlier removal, and loss condition monitoring are necessary to help the algorithm converge to a physical model.

The Gaussian process regression framework underlying GAP provides an uncertainty quantification that qualitatively estimates the potential’s accuracy for any given atomic configuration.

The DeePMD model successfully reproduces the superionic behavior of solid-state electrolytes with linear Lithium/Sodium mean squared displacement over time and diffusion coefficient uncertainty of about 20% or smaller, which is precise enough for battery applications.
The DeePMD model provides excellent energy conservation in all tested systems up to 2 ns of NVE dynamics.
For NASICON, training starting from PFF-MD configurations with 480 atoms achieves convergence during the first training loop with activation energy around 0.2 eV.
For NASICON, training starting from FPMD configurations with 80 atoms fails to converge even after three training loops with activation energies spanning 0.2-0.4 eV.
Starting the training loop with PFF-MD configurations leads to faster convergence than starting with short FPMD trajectories because larger simulation cells can be used.

The proposed training protocol based on augmenting the training set via intermediate molecular dynamics simulations can assess the quality of approximate trajectories and computed physical properties.
The DeePMD model is a promising candidate for developing a universal potential for solid-state electrolytes, though care must be taken when selecting training configurations.
For LLZO, results are quite insensitive to the choice of cell volume (NPT equilibrated vs experimental cif-file values) for producing the initial training set.

DeePMD reproduces AIMD energies, forces, and virial tensors for water and ice with root‑mean‑square errors of approximately 1 meV per molecule for energy, 40 meV Å⁻¹ for forces, and 1–2 meV for the virial.
DeePMD accurately reproduces radial distribution functions and three‑body angular distribution functions of liquid water and ice, matching AIMD results.
For a diverse set of organic molecules, DeePMD achieves lower mean absolute errors in both energy and forces than the GDML benchmark.
The computational cost of DeePMD scales linearly with the number of atoms and is several orders of magnitude lower than equivalent AIMD simulations, comparable to empirical force fields.
A DeePMD model trained on relatively small systems (64–96 water or ice molecules) can be directly applied to much larger systems without loss of accuracy, demonstrating strong transferability.
In principle, DeePMD could be trained on chemically accurate data from high‑level quantum chemistry or quantum Monte Carlo, extending its applicability beyond density‑functional theory.

Combined two-body, three-body, and SOAP many-body descriptors are necessary for GAP to achieve the accuracy limit imposed by force locality and make physically meaningful predictions; models using only subsets of descriptors produce unphysical structures during molecular dynamics simulations.

The modified convolution function reduces the mean absolute error for formation‑energy prediction from 0.112 eV/atom to 0.039 eV/atom, achieving DFT‑level accuracy comparable to the experimental DFT‑experiment error of 0.081–0.136 eV/atom.
CGCNN classifies metals versus semiconductors with an area under the ROC curve of 0.95 and an overall accuracy of 0.90.

By extracting per‑atom site energies in perovskites, the model reveals that large‑radius elements stabilize the A site and group 4‑6 elements stabilize the B site, and using these insights the high‑throughput search space for stable perovskites is reduced by a factor of seven (from 18,928 to 228 candidates).

When applied to a set of 1,585 crystals with elastic properties, CGCNN predicts bulk modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.077 log(GPa) and shear modulus with a mean absolute error of 0.114 log(GPa), demonstrating good generalization.
Using roughly 10⁴ training examples, CGCNN attains DFT‑level accuracy for eight distinct material properties across diverse crystal types and compositions.

Compared with a prior statistical‑learning approach, CGCNN achieves similar or lower root‑mean‑square errors for bulk modulus (0.075 log(GPa) vs 0.105) and shear modulus (0.127 log(GPa) vs 0.138) using the same training data.

Machine‑learning models trained on Classical Force‑field Inspired Descriptors (CFID) achieve high predictive accuracy for formation energies, exfoliation energies, band gaps, magnetic moments, refractive indices, dielectric constants, thermoelectric performance, and piezoelectric/infrared modes.
Comparisons of JARVIS‑DFT computed formation energies, band gaps, and elastic constants with experimental measurements show acceptable error margins, confirming the database’s predictive reliability.
JARVIS‑FF automatically computes bulk modulus, defect formation energies, and phonon spectra for each force‑field and compares them with DFT results to assess force‑field quality.
SchNet provides rotationally invariant energy predictions and rotationally equivariant, energy‑conserving force predictions by defining forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy.

When trained on MD17 trajectories with a combined energy‑and‑force loss, SchNet achieves energy MAE ≤0.12 kcal/mol and force MAE ≤0.33 kcal/mol/Å, matching or surpassing GDML and DTNN on all tested molecules, including flexible ones such as malonaldehyde and ethanol.
Training SchNet with forces on only 1,000 examples yields better accuracy than training on 50,000 examples using energies alone, demonstrating that force information improves data efficiency.

On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training.
Including force information in the training loss causally improves SchNet’s generalization to previously unseen chemical structures in ISO17.
GDML cannot be trained on 50,000 MD17 examples due to its quadratic scaling with the number of atoms and samples, whereas SchNet scales to that dataset size.
Using a shifted softplus activation guarantees an infinitely differentiable (smooth) potential energy surface, facilitating geometry optimization.
Continuous-filter convolutions produce smoother energy predictions than discrete filters, as illustrated in Figure 1.
On the QM9 benchmark, SchNet attains a mean absolute error of 0.31 kcal/mol for total‑energy prediction with 110 k training examples, outperforming DTNN (0.84) and enn‑s2s (0.45).

For internal energy at 0 K (U0), enthalpy (H), Gibbs free energy (G), heat capacity at constant volume (Cv), and highest vibrational frequency (Ω), the MPNN records lower mean absolute errors than SchNet and DTNN (U0 MAE 0.45 vs 0.55/0.72; H 0.39 vs 0.59/0.80; G 0.44 vs 0.55/0.74; Cv 0.80 vs 0.99/1.71; Ω 0.19 vs 0.41/0.78).
Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation‑equivariant forces.
The applied plane-wave kinetic energy cut-off (Ecut) is the largest recommended value among all species in the calculation, increased by a factor of 1.4.

The first RELAX calculation is performed in collinear spin-polarized fashion with initial magnetic moments set to 1.0 µB per atom, and spin polarization is turned off in subsequent calculations if magnetization is below 0.025 µB/atom.

Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.
For LLZO, the computed activation energies range from 0.2 to 0.22 eV, in very good agreement with experimental values of 0.20-0.21 eV for cubic LLZO.
For LGPS, the computed activation energy is 0.16 eV, which is slightly lower than experimental values (0.22 eV) but in line with previous computational studies (0.17-0.21 eV).
The number of force components in the initial training set is more important than total configurations for obtaining generalizable models.
MEGNet models achieve lower mean absolute errors than SchNet on 11 of the 13 QM9 molecular properties evaluated.

Simple MEGNet models that use only atomic number and spatial distance as input achieve chemical accuracy, perform comparably to full‑feature models, and outperform prior state‑of‑the‑art models on 8 of the 13 QM9 properties.

MEGNet models trained on approximately 60,000 crystals outperform prior models (SchNet and CGCNN) for formation energy, band gap, bulk modulus, and shear modulus, achieving errors comparable to or better than density‑functional‑theory uncertainties.

A unified free‑energy MEGNet model that incorporates temperature, pressure, and entropy as global state inputs predicts U₀, U, H, and G with a combined mean absolute error of 0.010 eV, comparable to separate single‑property models.
Ensembling two independently trained three‑block MEGNet models lowers the formation‑energy mean absolute error from 0.028 eV/atom to 0.024 eV/atom.
Increasing the number of MEGNet blocks improves accuracy for properties that depend on longer‑range interactions, such as zero‑point vibrational energy, electronic spatial extent, and dipole moment.
Increasing the crystal graph radius cut‑off from 4 Å to 6 Å slightly worsens the formation‑energy mean absolute error (to 0.03 eV/atom), confirming the 4 Å cut‑off as near‑optimal.

The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
At the lowest order, the magnetic ACE reproduces a distance‑dependent Heisenberg interaction.

Representing tensors with spherical harmonics yields a dramatically sparser basis, where a rank‑N Cartesian tensor with 3^N components can be represented by (N+1)^2 spherical harmonics (e.g., a 10th‑order tensor requires 121 harmonics instead of 59 049 Cartesian components).
Moments Tensor Potentials (MTP) and the Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential (SNAP) can be expressed exactly as special cases of the ACE.

Neglecting spin‑orbit coupling forces all magnetic angular momenta to be zero, greatly reducing the number of ACE expansion coefficients, since the magnetic contribution to the cohesive energy is only about 10 % of the total.
The ACE formulation is invariant under translation, rotation, inversion and permutation of identical atoms.
Although the full magnetic and charge‑transfer ACE contains many parameters, hierarchical ordering of interactions allows robust and systematic fitting to reference data.
Implementing the extended ACE for vectorial, tensorial, magnetic and charge degrees of freedom requires no significantly greater effort than the original scalar ACE implementation.

L1-bal000047.surface_form: Atomic cluster expansion of scalar, vectorial and tensorial properties and including magnetism and charge transfer
Ralf Drautz

The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
At the lowest order, the magnetic ACE reproduces a distance‑dependent Heisenberg interaction.
Moments Tensor Potentials (MTP) and the Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential (SNAP) can be expressed exactly as special cases of the ACE.

Neglecting spin‑orbit coupling forces all magnetic angular momenta to be zero, greatly reducing the number of ACE expansion coefficients, since the magnetic contribution to the cohesive energy is only about 10 % of the total.
The ACE formulation is invariant under translation, rotation, inversion and permutation of identical atoms.
Although the full magnetic and charge‑transfer ACE contains many parameters, hierarchical ordering of interactions allows robust and systematic fitting to reference data.
Implementing the extended ACE for vectorial, tensorial, magnetic and charge degrees of freedom requires no significantly greater effort than the original scalar ACE implementation.
Because the ACE basis is complete and hierarchical, it can in principle achieve arbitrary accuracy for any scalar, vectorial or tensorial property.
DeePMD preserves translational, rotational, and permutational symmetries by constructing a local reference frame for each atom and sorting neighbor lists by species and inverse distance.

node:clai_00520.surface_form: The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.

node:clai_00521.surface_form: The derived ACE formulas enable efficient evaluation of forces and magnetic torques.

node:clai_00522.surface_form: At the lowest order, the magnetic ACE reproduces a distance‑dependent Heisenberg interaction.

node:clai_00523.surface_form: Representing tensors with spherical harmonics yields a dramatically sparser basis, where a rank‑N Cartesian tensor with 3^N components can be represented by (N+1)^2 spherical harmonics (e.g., a 10th‑order tensor requires 121 harmonics instead of 59 049 Cartesian components).

node:clai_00524.surface_form: Moments Tensor Potentials (MTP) and the Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential (SNAP) can be expressed exactly as special cases of the ACE.

node:clai_00525.surface_form: Neglecting spin‑orbit coupling forces all magnetic angular momenta to be zero, greatly reducing the number of ACE expansion coefficients, since the magnetic contribution to the cohesive energy is only about 10 % of the total.

node:clai_00526.surface_form: The ACE formulation is invariant under translation, rotation, inversion and permutation of identical atoms.

node:clai_00527.surface_form: Although the full magnetic and charge‑transfer ACE contains many parameters, hierarchical ordering of interactions allows robust and systematic fitting to reference data.

node:clai_00528.surface_form: Implementing the extended ACE for vectorial, tensorial, magnetic and charge degrees of freedom requires no significantly greater effort than the original scalar ACE implementation.

node:clai_00529.surface_form: Because the ACE basis is complete and hierarchical, it can in principle achieve arbitrary accuracy for any scalar, vectorial or tensorial property.

node:clai_00557.surface_form: The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals.

node:clai_00558.surface_form: The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%.

node:clai_00559.surface_form: The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa).

node:clai_00560.surface_form: In polycrystalline aluminum, the GNN predicts atomic potential energy with a mean normalized relative error of 11.0% (maximum ≈13%) and achieves R² = 0.99 for mean potential energy versus grain number.

node:clai_00561.surface_form: Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene.

node:clai_00562.surface_form: The GNN’s stress predictions are substantially more accurate than on‑the‑fly stress calculations from the force field, which exhibit higher errors.

node:clai_00563.surface_form: The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples.

node:clai_00564.surface_form: Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations.

node:clai_00565.surface_form: The GNN respects physical constraints, accurately capturing derivative properties such as stress fields that obey underlying physical laws, and predicts global properties (Young’s modulus, total potential energy) that follow known physical relationships and match MD results across different crystalline systems.

node:clai_00566.surface_form: The Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA) GNN model achieves the lowest mean and variance of test mean‑squared error among GCN, GAT, and MPNN (sum and max) variants on the polycrystalline graphene dataset.

node:clai_00567.surface_form: The GNN accelerates atomic property prediction by hundreds to thousands of times compared with conventional MD simulations, requiring seconds on a single CPU versus thousands of seconds on 24 CPUs.

node:clai_00568.surface_form: Linear fitting of atomic properties yields substantially higher prediction errors than the GNN approach, demonstrating the superiority of the nonlinear GNN model for mapping initial structures to final property distributions.

node:clai_00569.surface_form: DeePMD reproduces AIMD energies, forces, and virial tensors for water and ice with root‑mean‑square errors of approximately 1 meV per molecule for energy, 40 meV Å⁻¹ for forces, and 1–2 meV for the virial.

node:clai_00570.surface_form: DeePMD accurately reproduces radial distribution functions and three‑body angular distribution functions of liquid water and ice, matching AIMD results.

node:clai_00571.surface_form: For a diverse set of organic molecules, DeePMD achieves lower mean absolute errors in both energy and forces than the GDML benchmark.

node:clai_00572.surface_form: The computational cost of DeePMD scales linearly with the number of atoms and is several orders of magnitude lower than equivalent AIMD simulations, comparable to empirical force fields.

node:clai_00573.surface_form: A DeePMD model trained on relatively small systems (64–96 water or ice molecules) can be directly applied to much larger systems without loss of accuracy, demonstrating strong transferability.

node:clai_00574.surface_form: DeePMD preserves translational, rotational, and permutational symmetries by constructing a local reference frame for each atom and sorting neighbor lists by species and inverse distance.

node:clai_00575.surface_form: Using a loss function with adaptive prefactors that emphasize forces early and energies/virial later reduces the total training time to a few core‑hours for all test cases.

node:clai_00576.surface_form: Discontinuities in forces caused by the sharp cutoff radius and neighbor‑list sorting are much smaller than thermal fluctuations and do not impair canonical sampling.

node:clai_00577.surface_form: In principle, DeePMD could be trained on chemically accurate data from high‑level quantum chemistry or quantum Monte Carlo, extending its applicability beyond density‑functional theory.

node:clai_00578.surface_form: DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.

node:clai_00579.surface_form: DeepH-E3 predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with sub‑meV mean absolute error, reducing the error by roughly a factor of two compared with the original DeepH method across diverse material systems.

node:clai_00580.surface_form: DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.

node:clai_00581.surface_form: DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.

node:clai_00582.surface_form: DeepH‑E3 predicts a spin‑orbit‑coupling‑induced topological quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi₂Te₃, evidenced by band‑gap closing and reopening and a change of the Z₂ invariant from 0 to 1 as SOC strength increases.

node:clai_00583.surface_form: DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.

node:clai_00584.surface_form: DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.

node:clai_00585.surface_form: The model generalizes to arbitrarily twisted bilayer structures; the mean absolute error of Hamiltonian predictions decreases as the Moiré supercell size grows (or twist angle decreases).

node:clai_00586.surface_form: The equivariant architecture handles spin‑orbital Hamiltonians by separating real and imaginary components and applying a change‑of‑basis for half‑integer representations, thereby preserving equivariance without requiring complex‑valued network layers.

node:clai_00587.surface_form: The model can fit 2.8 × 10⁹ non‑zero complex‑valued Hamiltonian matrix elements with only ~10⁵ real trainable parameters, indicating high capacity efficiency.

node:clai_00639.surface_form: The final M3GNet interatomic potential achieves test mean absolute errors of 0.035 eV/atom for energy, 0.072 eV/Å for forces, and 0.41 GPa for stresses on a held‑out Materials Project dataset covering 89 elements.

node:clai_00640.surface_form: Relaxing test crystals with M3GNet reduces median volume error from 2.4 % to 0.6 % and energy mean absolute error from 0.169 eV/atom to 0.035 eV/atom relative to DFT‑relaxed references.

node:clai_00641.surface_form: A single‑CPU M3GNet relaxation completes in about 22 seconds, compared with 15 hours on 32 cores for DFT; pre‑relaxation with M3GNet shortens subsequent DFT relaxation time by roughly a factor of three and reduces total CPU time by an average factor of 2.97.

node:clai_00642.surface_form: Screening 31.7 million hypothetical crystals with M3GNet identifies approximately 1.8 million candidates with predicted hull distances below 0.001 eV/atom, and among the 2,000 lowest‑energy candidates, 1,578 are confirmed stable (Ehull < 0.001 eV/atom) by DFT.

node:clai_00646.surface_form: M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.

node:clai_00647.surface_form: On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.

node:clai_00648.surface_form: Across nine MatBench structural property datasets, M3GNet yields lower mean absolute errors than MODNet, AtomSets‑V1, MEGNet, and AutoMatminer, with improvements of 20.5 %–41.3 % on large datasets such as perovskite formation energy and MP band gap, and demonstrates excellent prediction accuracy on the broader MatBench suite.

node:clai_00649.surface_form: For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation‑of‑state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long‑range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.

node:clai_00650.surface_form: The M3GNet architecture preserves continuity of energies, forces, and stresses with respect to changes in bond count, satisfying a necessary physical constraint for interatomic potentials.
